chunks: From him, from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan, from his father, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz, from Zurārah, from one of the two عليهما السلام, who said:
I asked him about a menstruating woman with whom her husband has intercourse. He said: Nothing is due upon him; he should seek Allah’s forgiveness and not return to it.

Thus, the proper way regarding these reports is that they are to be understood as referring to when the man did not know from her condition that she was menstruating; then nothing is binding upon him. But as for when he knows that, then expiation is binding upon him according to what we have mentioned.

And no one may say: This interpretation is not possible, because if these reports were to be understood as applying to the state of forgetfulness, he عليه السلام would not have said, “He seeks forgiveness from his Lord for what he did,” nor that “he disobeyed his Lord.” For it is not impossible to apply the statement to him that he disobeyed, nor to urge him to seek forgiveness, inasmuch as he was negligent in asking about her condition and whether she was menstruating or not, while knowing that had she been menstruating, intercourse with her would have been forbidden to him. So by this negligence he is disobedient, and seeking forgiveness becomes obligatory upon him.

What clarifies this interpretation is the report of Layth al-Murādī mentioned earlier. He said: I asked Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man having intercourse with his wife while she was menstruating by mistake. So he restricted the question by stating that his intercourse with her had been in error, and he عليه السلام answered him: Nothing is due upon him, though he has disobeyed his Lord.

key_terms.التَّفْرِيطِ: negligence or culpable failure to exercise due care
key_terms.الْكَفَّارَةُ: the expiation due for the violation

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a man has intercourse with his wife while she is menstruating, knowingly or unknowingly?
ai.summary: This report discusses the ruling on intercourse with a menstruating wife and explains that when the man was unaware of her state, no expiation is due, though he must seek forgiveness. If he knew she was menstruating, then expiation is binding, and the text further explains that negligence in failing to ascertain her condition is itself blameworthy.
